#1486. Stephen Robinson was just the latest Aberdeen manager to crash and burn... it's time to look at the club and its structure

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026

Across the space of two days last week, Aberdeen fans were dragged down memory lane only to emerge bruised and battered for their troubles.

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of plain old Alex Ferguson’s departure to Manchester United. It was an occasion for newspapers and TV bulletins to again recall the mind-blowing feats which led to the biggest club in Britain beating a path to Pittodrie.

Three Scottish championships, four Scottish Cups, a League Cup, the Cup Winners’ Cup and the Super Cup. The redrawing of the landscape of Scottish football.

There was something especially brutal about how those glories were juxtaposed beside the struggles of the soon-to-be former Dons boss, Stephen Robinson, 24 hours later.

After eight months of grim toil in the Granite City, the four-goal home thrashing the Northern Irishman suffered at the hands of Hibernian on Saturday blew away any lingering hope he retained of turning an increasingly desperate situation around.

A proven manager who was always simply the wrong fit for Aberdeen, Robinson will lick his wounds and come again.

Stephen Robinson is a proven manager who was always the wrong fit  for Aberdeen

But while a failure to live up to Fergie’s impossibly high standards might have done for those in Robinson’s shoes in the years which immediately followed the great man’s move to Old Trafford, no Aberdeen supporter in their right mind views things through that prism these days.

The majority of those who watched Saturday’s capitulation weren’t even born when Fergie’s Reds were running rampage throughout Europe.

They appreciate that the slayings of Real Madrid and Bayern Munich which they watched on YouTube were the highlights of a golden era for the club. One they know is not coming back.

In 2026, the expectation is more modest and hardly unreasonable. That with the fifth-highest average crowd in the country, Aberdeen should be in the top six almost every year, frequently playing in Europe most seasons and winning the odd cup. Yet, they’re miles off that right now.

While Jimmy Thelin did deliver a day in the sun by beating Celtic in the Scottish Cup final last year, that success was an anomaly. There have been just two top-six finishes in the past five years, with two ninth-placed finishes and one in tenth spot.

Given all that, it’s difficult not to recall the old wisdom about being careful what you wished for.

In Derek McInnes’ eight seasons at the club between 2013 and 2021, the team never finished below fourth and were runners-up four years on the spin. The League Cup was also secured in 2014.

A run of consistency and success which supporters had long craved was soon forgotten. McInnes’ familiarity and loyalty were eventually held against him.

Five managers later, Aberdeen appear to be as far away from reclaiming their status as one of the Scottish game’s powerhouses as they’ve ever been.

‘I think we’ve been waiting on it for four or five years,’ said Gothenburg legend Alex McLeish.

‘There’s been some signs, obviously winning the cup that year. You think that’s a wee springboard for the coming season and then it’s all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league.’

As Robinson cleared his desk last night, even those fans who didn’t want him at the club in the first place would have been reluctant to hold him entirely responsible for the current ills.

The Northern Irishman is demonstrably a good manager. He guided St Mirren to three top-six finishes and the League Cup.

Thelin performed wonders across a long period at Elfsborg. Two years ago, he had Aberdeen sitting on top of the table.

Jim Goodwin was humiliated at Darvel, but now has buoyant Dundee United believing again.

Even Stephen Glass, a left-field choice to succeed McInnes, went on to enjoy success with Memphis 901 and as assistant to Robbie Keane at Ferencvaros.

When a club appoints one manager who doesn’t work out, it’s logical to question the individual. If five managers crash and burn, it says more about the environment and the structure they work in.

‘What is the solution?’ asked McLeish. ‘It’s definitely always down to what kind of players you’ve got.

Jimmy Thelin lifted the Scottish Cup before his Aberdeen career ended in disappointment

‘It’s trying to get a team to function together. To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, beat a man, playing one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality comes into it.

‘The manager will always get the worse side of it, you know, because they can’t sack 20 players.’

While it’s too late to save Robinson, the club do appear to have moved to address this particular shortcoming.

Back in March, Darren Mowbray returned to Pittodrie as head of recruitment three years on from his first stint which saw the captures of Bojan Miovski and Ylber Ramadani.

The trouble is that the mish-mash of players who were recruited by Jordan Miles, Chris Badlan and Nuno de Almeida are plainly not good enough.

Mowbray, it must be said, didn’t get too much right in the summer, either.

It’s not just the failure to sign players with the requisite pedigree and character which dismays the Aberdeen supporters.

When it was clear that Thelin’s time was up in January, the Swede was shown the door without there being a replacement waiting in the wings.

While there were legitimate reasons why Eirik Horneland couldn’t commit at that moment, the Dons’ hierarchy needed a Plan B.

Sandro Schwarz came to the Granite City for talks but nothing materialised, with Peter Leven remaining in interim charge.

With the pressure growing, Robinson – a wholly unpopular choice – was unveiled nine weeks and four days on. None of this reflected well on anyone involved.

Lutz Pfannenstiel, the sporting director, has written a book on his adventures in the game which included his recollections of the time he kept a penguin in his bath.

As Aberdeen’s hopes for the season have gone down the plughole, he’s not uttered a syllable in public.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel has had nothing to say during Aberdeen's recent troubles

With former FA bigwig Adrian Bevington now in the chief executive’s role, Pfannenstiel’s input into the recruitment of the new manager will be interesting.

And what role does Dave Cormack have to play? No one doubts the chairman’s passion for the club or his financial commitment to it.

But after seven years in the post, Pittodrie, on his watch, has acquired the unfortunate reputation of being a place where managers crash and burn. And you begin to suspect they might not be the sum total of the issues.

‘Dave Cormack is a close friend and I know he’s done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,’ said McLeish. ‘We saw that Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago, but the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘Dave will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong. You can’t sleep at night.

‘Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There’ll be a big burden on him right now.

‘He’s been stoic and he’s stood by the club. He has to have massive credit for that. It’s just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.’

Alex McLeish was speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org

#1480. The 10 players Tottenham let go in the summer – & how they’re faring elsewhere

There was a lot of focus on the players coming through the door, but Tottenham Hotspur also let a lot of players go this past summer.

Ten players left in the summer permanently with another seven out on loan, as Roberto De Zerbi reshaped his squad following last year’s relegation scare.

And so we’re catching up on how those permanent exits have gone.

This is already looking like one that got away.

Following the Van Hecke/Vuskovic swap deal, it is the latter that has looked the better this season and has played a starring role in Fabian Hurzeler’s impressive Brighton team.

He has started all 10 games for the Seagulls, missing just two minutes of action so far this season, and has all the attributes that you would want from a modern centre-back.

Spurs reportedly inserted a clause into the contract but that was only to match any accepted bid rather than a pre-determined amount. If he continues like this, Brighton would not want to sell him for anything but a huge fee.

Another centre-back that left Spurs in the summer was Christian Romero, who took his sometimes maybe good, sometimes maybe red card attitude to Spain.

Moving to Atletico seems to have served him well as he is now under the rule of ‘takes no s**t’ Diego Simeone.

He’s played eight games for the Madrid side so far, who are third in La Liga and have the joint best defence.

Plenty of English players have enjoyed trips abroad but Djed Spence has yet to make a real mark at Inter.

He missed the first five games as he came back to fitness following the World Cup and was phased into the team, rather than given a starting spot from the off.

He did start the Milan derby, which Inter lost 3-1 to Ruben Amorim’s Milan, but was trusted to start again the following game, providing an assist in a 2-0 win over Como.

Even after the arrival of Omar Marmoush and Savinho, Spurs’ forward line looks the weakest area of the team. If only they had access to a striker scoring for fun.

Yes, it’s the Championship but Will Lankshear’s 13 goals in 13 games for Middlesbrough is hugely impressive and the 21-year-old already looks like an England star of the future. Keep scoring at that rate and he may well get a call-up sooner rather than later.

Spurs sold him for around £20m which looks on the low side already.

If Spurs fans were annoyed about the sale of Lankshear, they were probably less unhappy with the transfer of Alejo Veliz.

Spurs fans would do well to pick him out of a lineup for he only played eight games for Tottenham since joining in 2023, amounting to 45 minutes in total.

He’s been on loan to both Espanyol and Rosario Central but moved permanently to Esporte Clube Bahia in Brazil.

The 23-year-old has got four goals in his 15 games for the club so far.

It was not just Lankshear who left Spurs for Middlesbrough as defender Phillips also made the same journey in the summer.

He had plenty of Championship experience having spent the past two seasons in the division on loan at Stoke but Middlesbrough signed him in the summer for an initial fee of £7m.

He has since become a key member of Kim Hellberg’s side. He also scored a last-minute winner in a 4-3 thriller against Norwich, which is a great way to endear yourself to the fans.

Having been on loan spells to three different clubs, Manor Solomon left Spurs permanently in the summer to join West Ham.

Given the number 10 shirt for the Hammers’ first season back in the Championship, he started well with a goal on his debut but has faded in the last few weeks.

West Ham have been on a terrible run too with him in the side, having failed to win the last four games he was involved in.

Another academy product let go is midfielder Devine, who has joined Preston.

It’s fair to say, Preston are stinking the gaff out in the Championship and are bottom, having won two games all season.

Devine has played in all but one match so far, although it took 11 games to register his first goal involvement. Preston did, though, pull off an upset against promotion candidates Southampton in their most recent game, so maybe their fortunes are starting to change.

Long-time youth product Dane Scarlett left in the summer having never managed to properly break into the Spurs first team.

He played 27 games for Spurs, of which 11 were in the Premier League for a combined 61 minutes, and has been out on loan here, there and everywhere.

He was most recently at Hibernian but has now joined Leyton Orient permanently. Since making the short trip, he’s got one goal in eight League One games.

The player most likely to give successive managers a migraine left Tottenham this summer and headed for Ajax.

He was unable to play for the first seven games due to visa issues and even then was only gradually brought into the team, with his debut being just eight minutes long.

He finally started in Ajax’s final game before the international break but was hooked on the hour mark.

#1479. Journey to Wembley: Halifax set sights on winning more fans and climbing mountain to the Football League as their FA Cup adventure is ended by route-one Cheltenham

By IAN HERBERT AT EV CHARGER POINTS STADIUM

Published: 21:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 18:05 EST, 9 November 2026

The FC Halifax manager John McGrath’s father-in-law is the top British mountaineer Alan Hinkes OBE and he knows that he has something of a summit of his own to scale, as he walks straight from the team bus to the pitch, set in the lee of Cheltenham’s mist-shrouded Cleeve Hill.

McGrath is all-too familiar with this setting. He brought his Buxton team here in the FA Cup's second round last season and was on the fringes of a major upset – 2-1 up at half-time – before watching the game fall away.

Cheltenham are a much stronger club, 12 months on, but our few weeks with McGrath, an Irishman who 25 years ago was playing for Aston Villa against Liverpool in the Premier League, reveal his ambition for the National League side he joined this summer.

We’re alongside him and FC Halifax on our journey to Wembley, told through all 13 rounds, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

A mist-veiled evening at Halifax’s Shay Stadium, a few weeks back, revealed much about 46-year-old McGrath. He arrives with his two-man coaching team for a Q&A with fans who, when the evening’s proceedings are finished, form a long and orderly queue to talk to him, one-on-one. The team’s four-hour drive to Southend awaits the following morning. But McGrath has no eye for the clock.

This managerial journey is one he hadn’t anticipated when, aged 32, a serious foot injury ended his long career with Burton Albion. He secured a master’s degree in broadcasting and media at Staffordshire University and had begun spots for Sky Sports and BBC local radio, yet here he is on ‘the grass’ he'd never wanted to leave.

His wife Fiona is Director of Public Realm at Islington Council and their time together is some weeks limited to a coffee at Doncaster station, near their home, when he drops her before daybreak. ‘It’s our little half an hour,’ he relates. ‘We’re ships that pass in the night.'

Cheltenham edged out FC Halifax 2-0 in front of 2,961 fans to reach round two

Cheltenham boss Steve Cotterill shakes hands with Halifax manager John McGrath

Ground staff put up the goalposts at EV Charger Points Stadium, also known as Whaddon Road

His club’s fans are partisan – 350 are here – and yearn for League Two, though there’s not a fortune at McGrath’s disposal. The club’s owner David Bosomworth was at the club when it went bust in 2008 and they say that experience left him painfully aware of the need for sustainability. Fair enough. Bosomworth has declined to speak to us. He is not at Cheltenham.

An hour out from kick-off, McGrath is handing out training vests for the warm-up as well as observing things – it’s a modest backroom team – and that defeat last season perhaps plays on his mind. ‘Cheltenham tweaked it that day and personally, I think I should have done the same,’ he says. ‘I’m a better manager, 12 months on.’

The club could badly use the £50,000 prize money that a win here would bring, not to mention the accompanying shot of exhilaration.

McGrath already belongs in the margins of the tournament’s history. He and his son, Jay, a Doncaster Rovers player, became the first father and son to play in the same team in an FA Cup game when McGrath, Mickleover Sports' player-manager for their preliminary-round win against Coventry Sphinx in 2019, fielded his 17-year-old boy.

Halifax seem up for this challenge. Their players go looking for their kit in their bus's luggage compartment before the driver has jumped out to produce the key. But Cheltenham have come a long way in the past year.

The former Burnley owner Mike Garlick bought the club 15 months ago and his investment strategy has echoes of the methods which made the Turf Moor club a Premier League side for seven out of eight years. Manager Steve Cotterill, quickly installed by Garlick, was briefly with him at Burnley.

Cheltenham fans arrive at the ground with their side riding high, fifth in League Two

Halifax fans cheer on their side but their Cup run is over - they travel to Kidderminster next Saturday in the National League

Mike Garlick bought Cheltenham last year and quickly installed Cotterill as manager

There’s an air of optimism around the place, as head groundsman Paul Gibson attends to some stray grass cuttings with a leaf blower and husband and wife team Gerry and Hannah Oldham sort the kit.

The ground staff, with their distinctive West Country burr, take enjoyment from several attempts at installing the goalposts before getting them upright. Mascot ‘Whaddney the Robin’ is limbering up for a leisurely lap of the stadium.

Garlick suggests we use Cotterill’s office as a quiet place to talk as the stadium begins to fill up. He tries calling the manager for his consent to do so but Cotterill’s phone rings out in the room.

It turns out Cotterill is receiving calls on his watch. This is a source of some humour as Cotterill eventually barrels into the office, exhibiting his usual energy. The two men clearly get on.

Extra preliminary round, August 8: Nelson 3-2 Stockport Georgians

Preliminary round, August 22: Witton Albion 1-0 Nelson

1st qualifying round, September 5: Avro 0-2 Witton Albion

2nd qualifying round, September 19: South Shields 7-0 Witton Albion

3rd qualifying round, October 3: Buxton 0-2 South Shields

4th qualifying round, October 17: Halifax 3-2 South Shields

1st round, November 7: Cheltenham Town 2-0 Halifax

Garlick looks more at home here than at Burnley. He also owns Spanish third-tier side Antequera CF and a club in Gibraltar but yearned for this kind of environment and Cheltenham, tumbling towards the EFL exit last year, badly needed help.

‘I missed English football,’ Garlick says. ‘I thought this was a club where I could make a difference and have some impact. When I came in, we had four points from nine games and were bottom of the league. It was hard work last season, but the fans seem happy for me to be here.

'Everyone who comes up to me says “thanks for helping the club,” which is nice. I never quite got that at Burnley to be honest. I’ve probably got more thanks here in 12 months than in 17 years on the board at Burnley. But that’s football isn’t it?!’

There’s been substantial investment in the training ground, a new stadium hospitality lounge, and Cotterill’s contacts have contributed to some eye-catching signings including veteran former Villa forward Andreas Weimann from Rapid Vienna.

Halifax start the game well, with wingers Ben Tollitt and Connor Douglas both flying and Conor Carty, the Irish forward who has been a revelation this season, ready to receive. Twice, they go close in the early stages. But Cotterill has a very uncomplicated route-one method in place and whip-fast striker Kirsten Otchere, on loan from Leicester City, looks lethal.

Will Flint’s string of fine interventions for Halifax is matched by the excellence of goalkeeper True Grant but Otchere crosses from the left for Jake Evans to score, left-footed.

This time McGrath does change things, adjusting the defensive line to quell Otchere’s threat after half time. Cotterill, whose colourful touchline antics include shoving his full-back out of the way when he blocks his line of view, grows concerned as Cheltenham’s attacking threat fades and Halifax dominate.

Carty nets from a Douglas’ crosses but is offside. Halifax lack the moment of class to convert superiority into goals. Substitute George Miller’s late header ended Halifax’s tournament for another year.

Halifax's Ben Tollitt battles for possession but his side cannot find a way through Cheltenham

McGrath and his Halifax players applaud the travelling supporters after their Cup exit

The Cheltenham fans flood out into suburban Whaddon Road fortified in their belief that something is building. ‘An FA Cup run is great for morale and also a massive contribution to the finances, because we’re hopefully going to strengthen again in January and the summer,’ says Garlick.

A foggy trip up the M6 awaits Halifax, though McGrath brings both a hinterland and perspective to the quest of start filling the famous old Shay Stadium once more and pushing closer to the fourth tier after 24 years away. His father-in-law was the first Briton to climb all the world's 8,000m mountains, in the Himalayan and Karakoram ranges of Nepal, Tibet and Pakistan.

‘He’s one of the best in the world,’ McGrath relates. ‘And however tough it is being a footballer or football manager, you try sitting on the side of Mount Everest for three months.

‘There’s a rumour building in our town that we play good football, that there’s goals to be seen at our stadium and a bunch of talented young men are representing the club in the right way.

'We want to get another 800 fans a week through the door and kick the club up the division and into the Football League. We think we can do that.’

#1476. Roma pursue Gittens for January

Roma continues to work ahead of the January transfer window, aiming to provide Gian Piero Gasperini with the attacking winger he’s long sought.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport reports, one of the names that has resurfaced is Jamie Gittens, who was already in talks this summer as part of the deal that could have brought Manu Koné to Chelsea.

The Londoners had offered the Englishman a loan deal worth nearly €60 million, but the Friedkins decided not to proceed, citing a lack of time to replace the Frenchman.

Now the deal could be reopened, as Gittens is unhappy with his limited playing time at Chelsea, where he’s only played 55 minutes in two appearances this season, both in the Carabao Cup.

The English club could consider a loan move, while still believing in the player’s qualities. Roma likes him for his speed, one-on-one ability, and dynamism, although recent physical problems, including an ankle injury and a hamstring injury, require some reflection.

#1475. Ranking 12 of Zlatan Ibrahimovic’s best goals in order of ridiculousness

Zlatan Ibrahimovic scored over 500 goals during his career, but it’s not so much the number of goals he scored that made him special as the outrageous way in which he scored them.

After spells with Juventus, Barcelona and Manchester United, Ibrahimovic continued to prove that he can score in ways which appear physically impossible before finally hanging up his boots at the end of the 2022-23 campaign.

Over his illustrious career, he built quite a catalogue of absurd goals. And now we’ve ranked just some of his most outrageous ones in order of ridiculousness.

Because this is Zlatan, it looks like a standard goal. Straightforward. Run of the mill.

But wait for the replay and see how high the ball is when Zlatan strikes it; how he twists his body; how he uses the outside of his boot to get it through the crowd and inside the post.

It’s bottom of our list, but a fine example of Zlatan making the extraordinary look ordinary.

﻿

When coaches tell you to “put your foot through it”, they probably mean something like this.

For Inter Milan, Ibrahimovic shows us the devastating consequence of mixing power with accuracy.

﻿

Ibrahimovic gets across the defender man-marking him and bullets the ball into the roof of the net – with the side of his boot, no less.

GOAL OF THE DAY :23’ : Zlatan Ibrahimović vs Olympique de Marseille (2-2)Ligue 1 2013-2014 – 8ème journée pic.twitter.com/7gb6hQptRU

— Jeunesse PSG (@psgfans18) March 20, 2018

Ibrahimovic has more or less standardised this move to the point of us no longer being surprised when he pulls it off, but at the time, when he was playing for Jose Mourinho’s Inter, it was something never witnessed before.

Ibrahimovic stands tall and lets the ball drop into his midriff. In a move we have now seen several times, he somehow generates enough power to send the ball into the top corner despite facing away from the goal.

GOAL OF THE DAY⚽️:10’: Zlatan Ibrahimović vs SC Bastia (victoire 4-0)@Ligue1Conforama 2013/2014 – 10ème journée pic.twitter.com/qIkAhGeRoh

— Jeunesse PSG (@psgfans18) April 8, 2018

A disgustingly good strike from distance. We don’t know what’s more ridiculous: the fact Ibrahimovic decided to strike the ball first time or the fact he manages to put so much whip on the ball.

﻿

Against Ronald Koeman’s Benfica in a pre-season encounter, eyes turned away from Juventus’ gorgeous kit for a moment as Ibrahimovic scored this delightful goal.

The ball isn’t in an ideal place for a strike, but Ibrahimovic pulls the trigger regardless and catches the keeper off guard from distance.

Even Gianluigi Buffon didn’t know what to do when Zlatan pulled off a swinging backheel kick in the Euro 2004 group stage match.

Very few players would have the wherewithal to even think of doing this. Even fewer would be able to pull it off.

Ibrahimović is the only player to appear twice in this thread.pic.twitter.com/LTd83ImyQ5

— GoalScorer Challenge (@GoalscorerC) June 12, 2020

First, Ibrahimovic turns the defender on the halfway line with a flick. Then he chases down the ball and shoulder-barges the pursuing defender to the floor.

This is all before the big Swede brings the ball into his control and slams it high past the goalkeeper at his near post.

﻿

In a match billed as the ‘California Classico’, this wasn’t a bad way for Ibrahimovic to score his 500th career goal.

"I’m happy for Toronto as they’ll be remembered as my 500th victim."

Ibrahimovic's 500th career goal was typically ridiculous.pic.twitter.com/7fkpKPWqvk

— Planet Football (@planetfutebol) June 5, 2023

Ibrahimovic hit the world stage with this goal.

Its ridiculousness stems from him beating the entire backline – including the same player twice – in such a short space, before coolly slotting the ball into the net and wheeling away in celebration. It’s so good we wrote an entire article about it.

﻿

In a list full of outrageous goals, this must be the most ridiculous of all. It was an overhead kick from 30 yards, FFS.

#OnThisDay in 2012, Zlatan Ibrahimovic did something which, let's face it, only he can do. That thirty-odd yard overhead kick against England. Sizzled Joe Hart's brain in his head like it was a fried egg. Sensational. pic.twitter.com/Wj7vmmBB8n

— MUNDIAL (@MundialMag) November 14, 2020

#1474. Roma and Ndicka to discuss possible new contract

Even in football, there are Batmans and Robins. Some are more likely to steal the show, while others remain quiet and behind the scenes, yet they perform a crucial role.

This is the case with Ndicka, who may not have Mancini’s grit or Hermoso’s charisma, but whose consistency is the (silent) leader of Roma’s defensive line.

The numbers speak for themselves, but above all, the facts. Evan has a solid resume.

Evan is a key figure despite the transfer rumors that rage every summer. He arrived on a free transfer in 2023, and his sale would generate a capital gain that would be useful for revitalizing the club’s coffers.

But in the end, he has always stayed despite some (timid) sirens from the Premier League, writes Daniele Aloisi in Il Messaggero.

In June, however, sporting director D’Amico’s duties will include sitting down with him to discuss a renewal. Ndicka has separated from his agent and is looking after his own interests.

His contract expires in 2028, and Roma will have to decide whether to extend it or let him go so as not to lose him for free twelve months later.

There’s no automatic renewal clause, but the center-back will receive 20% of the fee the club receives from his eventual sale.

Ultimately, it’s no good to anyone to leave on a free transfer. Evan is happy in the capital, and Gasp has no intention of losing one of his “gladiators.” Discussions will be postponed until next year.

#1473. Crystal Palace: Four signings that would be perfect for Thomas Frank in January

Thomas Frank is set to replace Pierre Sage as the manager of Crystal Palace and will be aiming to turn their fortunes around.

Palace are bottom of the table and have shown serious signs of decline this season after the loss of Oliver Glasner in the dugout. Sage just wasn’t able to get the same kind of results as his predecessor over his short reign and has paid the price early.

All Palace can hope now is that they’ve appointed Brentford Frank rather than Tottenham Frank. It could be an ideal opportunity for him to get back on track and redeem his reputation.

But he’ll need all the help he can get to turn this around.

Under Sage, Palace have had comfortably the worst defensive record in the Premier League, conceding 24 goals after 10 games.

Losing their two best centre-backs in successive transfer windows in 2026 hasn’t helped. Marc Guehi went to Manchester City in January before Maxence Lacroix joined Chelsea in the summer.

Palace have failed to replace them adequately. They’ve brought in a couple of temporary solutions on loan but need to think about the long term.

They might have to be savvy in January to find a good solution, looking beyond the usual places.

One player they’ve been linked with recently is Lecce defender Gabriel, who would be a good fit for Frank’s tactics if they can win the race.

Good in the air and alert when the ball’s on the ground, the 21-year-old is ready for his next step and a Premier League move could suit.

During his time at Brentford, Frank was able to help plenty of players improve and Gabriel could be the right kind of defender to work with in the short and long term.

Frank was delighted to sign Gallagher for Spurs last January. He won’t have been so delighted to be sacked four weeks later.

But with Gallagher falling behind in importance for Spurs this season, could he become available again?

If so, he could bring fresh energy into the Palace midfield. Adam Wharton hasn’t quite looked the same player there this season and could probably use some help to get back to his usual standards.

Gallagher could easily do the legwork. He also knows what it takes to play for Palace after impressing there on loan from Chelsea during the 2021-22 season, a spell that included eight goals from 39 games.

Palace could also do with improving their attack. Jean-Philippe Mateta is clearly unsettled, Jorgen Strand Larsen hasn’t got going and Eddie Nketiah isn’t up to scratch either.

Could Richarlison be worth a call? He’s been completely frozen out by Spurs, where Frank had a better opinion of him than Roberto De Zerbi does.

It’s anyone’s guess what Richarlison wants as his next step. But going to Palace would allow him to link back up with a familiar manager and stay in London, too.

The Brazilian is versatile enough to play as a lone striker or in support of another if Palace want to persist with Strand Larsen, Mateta or Nketiah as well.

If Frank wants to look further back, to happier times with Brentford, he might have a hard time convincing anyone to reunite with him given the current positions of both clubs.

But considering Hickey isn’t starting regularly for Brentford, with Michael Kayode ahead of him in the hierarchy at right-back, we wonder if he might be tempted.

Frank rated Hickey highly during their time together. It’s easy to forget the versatile full-back is still only 24.

Palace had to replace Daniel Munoz this summer and his successor Anan Khalaili has been hit and miss so far. Hickey would be someone Frank could trust to offer more security at wing-back.

Frank shut the door on a Brentford exit for Hickey before but what if he turned out to be the man to get him out of the Gtech Community Stadium after all?

#1472. 'I've never revealed the whole story': England fans wouldn't boo me if they knew the truth, says Ben White... as he defends World Cup walkout and rejecting call-ups

Published: 15:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 18:20 EST, 9 November 2026

Ben White believes England fans would not boo him if they knew the truth behind his 2022 World Cup walkout.

The Arsenal defender left the camp in Qatar after the group stages citing 'personal reasons', although a fallout with Gareth Southgate's assistant, Steve Holland, was later reported. He then declined a return to the England set-up while Southgate and Holland were in charge but was included by Thomas Tuchel in March of this year.

However, White was booed by fans inside Wembley when he came on in the second-half of a friendly against Uruguay, only to score his first international goal and then concede a late penalty in a 1-1 draw. He was not selected for the World Cup in North America but is back with the squad ahead of this week's Nations League fixtures against Croatia and Spain.

And the 29-year-old, addressing those jeers for the first time, said: 'It was hard to hear, especially because they didn't know the situation, which is kind of what I put my mind to.

'They don't know my situation and it is not really about what I have done, because they don't know why, and if they did they would not be booing or saying these things. I just think about maybe (them) not knowing the full story, and if they did, maybe they wouldn't (boo).'

He added: 'Obviously, a load has been said. I've probably seen all of it. I just think people don't know the full story, because I've never said anything, and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

Ben White has insisted he would not be booed by England fans if they knew the truth behind his World Cup walkout

White fell out with former England assistant Steve Holland (left) before heading home during the 2022 World Cup

'There were loads of things that happened and communication wasn't great. I don't want to throw anyone under the bus. A lot of people try to do that to me so it's something I wouldn't want to do myself. I think it's probably the best way. It's a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it's amazing to be here now. It's a privilege to be called up.'

White, however, is adamant that he would make the same decision today and leave the World Cup, even if he will not divulge the reasons as to why.

'I don't think I would (do anything different),' he said. 'I think, as a person, I'm quite real, and I made the decision that I would probably continue to make. It's one that I'm not happy about. It wasn't ideal. But it happened, it's time to move on.

'I don't think I am looking to win anyone over or say anything that helps them get back on my side. It is what it is. There are reasons for it and I am just looking forward to playing for England and doing well and looking for success.'

White has spoken publicly about not watching football, and this, too, has been used against him by some supporters.

'It doesn't mean I don't like football, because I do it every day, so I must like it a little bit!' he said. 'It's because I don't watch it, which I think is quite normal for someone that does a job and then doesn't go home and then continue watching that job.

'I don't think anyone knows my personality. I keep that to my loved ones and family. It's all noise when people have an opinion on that stuff. It is not actually me. People don't know me and I like it that way. You give so much to the game, which is intense. I think it's important to keep some bits for yourself. I keep the energy for the people I love.'

England new boy Josh King believes his aptitude for academia gives him an advantage at the start of a burgeoning career.

The Fulham star – who has two Premier League goals this season – linked up with Thomas Tuchel’s squad on Monday morning as one of two fresh call ups alongside Jobe Bellingham.

King was a straight-A student at the renowned independent Hampton School in south London, with alumni including Queen guitarist Sir Brian May and golf pro Paul Casey.

The teenager’s mother, Michelle, is a university lecturer and finishing a PhD on sickle cell disease while his father Steve is a personal injury lawyer.

‘The most important thing about being good academically and education-wise is you’re able to take on information much more quickly,’ King said.

‘You can take on information which might take a bit longer for other people. I think that definitely helps.’

While the 19-year-old was invited to take part in a pre-World Cup training camp in Miami, he is hoping to make his international bow against Croatia on Thursday.

Although a central figure in Fulham’s midfield, a confident King could be utilised wider by Tuchel were he to be given an opportunity across the two-game Nations League camp.

‘There was a buzz around Fulham when I got called up [this week],’ he added. ‘I got off the phone with the boss, ran into the kitchen and started cheering with my dad. I called mum at work and she was screaming in the office. This felt slightly unachievable when I was younger.’

Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were namechecked as those who helped him settle when introduced to the group in Florida, with King having also studied the likes of Jamal Musiala and Pedri to elevate his own game.

‘The main thing you take is the standards they set,’ he said when reflecting on joining the camp in America. ‘The way they conduct themselves, the way they perform every day, the way they train and the way they take everything seriously.

‘The little things, technical things, the way some people strike the ball, the way some people pass, just little things which you almost take without thinking about it - they also have an impact.

‘On a few occasions I asked “how do you finish this way” or “what do you do in this scenario” and it always helps to add to my game.’

#1469. 18 more England records Harry Kane could break after becoming all-time caps leader

Harry Kane. The most-capped England player of all time and the top scorer for his country too. He might just be his nation’s best ever representative, you know.

Sure, he wasn’t around for the World Cup win in 1966. But when that’s the only major honour England have ever won, you can’t exactly knock players down for not replicating it.

With someone like Kane, you just have to look at the numbers to realise what he’s achieved. More often than not, he passes the eye test as well. He’s been a huge influence for England at some tournaments over the years.

And now, after his cap against Croatia on Thursday, he’s played in more England internationals than anyone else. A whole 126 of them.

Kane can proudly boast the all-time appearance and goal records for England, which are the big two. He also holds the records for most appearances as captain, most appearances at the Euros, most caps and goals while playing for a foreign club, most goals in a calendar year and so on.

But there are still more he could break. He’s 33 now, but still in good shape. Come on, this is the reigning Ballon d’Or winner we’re talking about.

So here are some records that could be in his sights over the rest of his international career.

Kane’s already a joint-record holder for this one and, unlike the three old-timers he shares the record with, he’s done it twice.

The record is six, first set by Tinsley Lindley in the 1880s and since matched by Jimmy Windridge in the 1900s, Tommy Lawton in the 1930s and Kane in both 2019 and between December 2022 and June 2023.

Steve Bloomer, from the 1890s, has the record of scoring in 10 consecutive appearances, but there were fixtures he didn’t play in in between.

So Kane is one of the four record holders for most consecutive England games scored in – and he’s not far off doing it for a third time.

He’s scored in every England game since the World Cup and so is currently on a run of five. All he needs to do is score against Spain on Sunday and then in England’s first game of the March international break to become the first man to score in seven consecutive England fixtures.

The next tournament England will be turning their attention to qualifying for is Euro 2028. And yes, they have to qualify, despite being co-hosts.

Kane is already a few days older than the current record holder for the oldest England scorer in a Euros qualifying match – Kyle Walker at 33 years and 104 days – and he’s going to score at least once in qualifying, right?

Should England make it to Euro 2028, you’d imagine Kane would still be an important player by then.

It’d be his fourth Euros with England, enough for him to overtake the eight players he’s currently level with. The only other among them still active in international football is Jordan Henderson, but we see Kane as a safer bet to be in the squad by then.

The next Euros would also be the seventh consecutive tournament Kane had represented England at. He’s currently tied with Henderson, Sol Campbell and Wayne Rooney on six in a row.

Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old when Euro 2028 kicks off. It won’t make him the oldest player to represent England at the tournament – that’s goalkeeper Peter Shilton at 38 – but he would be the oldest outfield player, presuming no one older than him would be in the squad.

Only Henderson and Dan Burn were older than him in the World Cup squad and we’d be a bit surprised if they were still sticking around for the next tournament.

The current record is held by Stuart Pearce at 34 years and 63 days old.

Surely Kane has at least one more goal in him at the Euros, even if we are looking 18 months into the future here.

If he does, he’d overtake Alan Shearer, who he’s currently tied with on seven, as England’s top scorer at the Euros. In fact, unless anyone was to get there before him, only Cristiano Ronaldo and Michel Platini would still be above him for the competition as a whole.

In the event of him scoring at Euro 2028, Kane would have a goal to his name from five consecutive international tournaments.

His only equivalent on four is Michael Owen.

And whenever that hypothetical Euros goal would come, Kane would be guaranteed to beat Trevor Brooking’s record as England’s oldest scorer at the competition.

Sir Trevor was 31 years old when he set the record, an age Kane is already past.

A bit more ambitious here, but the current record for most goals at a single Euros tournament by an Englishman is five, set by Alan Shearer in 1996.

It’s not that far out of reach, is it? Sure, only nine players have done it for any country before, but if England were to go far, there’d be enough games for Kane to have a crack at it.

He consistently steps up at the World Cup for his country and there’s no reason why he couldn’t at the Euros too. His personal best at the tournament is four in 2021, for the delayed 2020 edition.

And like Shearer in ’96, he’d have home advantage to carry him through as well.

File this one under unlikely, but maybe not as much as it sounds.

Onto the next tournament cycle and we could imagine a future in which Kane is still involved for the build-up to the 2030 World Cup.

He recently said it was “fairly realistic” that he’d still be an England player by the time of the next World Cup, but of course, England would have to get there first.

The current oldest scorer for England in a World Cup qualifying match is Teddy Sheringham, who was 35 years and 187 days old.

Details of the qualification process for the 2030 World Cup aren’t out yet, but Kane will turn 35 in the summer of 2028 and if he scores towards the end of a qualification campaign, he’d be able to surpass Sheringham.

If Kane does make it to the next World Cup, and plays for England at least once in every year in between, he’ll set a new record for the most consecutive years of appearances for the Three Lions.

2026 is the 12th consecutive year in which he’s appeared for his country. The record of 15 is currently shared by David Seaman and Rio Ferdinand.

As long as his England career continues uninterrupted, Kane will join them in 2029 and beat them in 2030.

Kane is already England’s top scorer at the World Cup, but he hasn’t played the most games at it for his country.

The record is Jordan Pickford’s with 19. Kane is one behind on 18.

There’s every chance both of them will be at the World Cup next time, but there’s half a suspicion Pickford could be phased out by then – especially if someone like James Trafford develops over the next few years.

A successor to Kane up front isn’t quite as obvious just yet and so he might be relied upon for longer, giving him a chance to overtake his long-time teammate.

The oldest scorer for England at a World Cup finals game was Tom Finney. He was 36 years and 64 days old when he scored against the Soviet Union in 1958.

Kane will be more than 250 days older than that by the time the next World Cup commences, so he’d just need a goal at any time to beat it.

Kane’s recent contract renewal with Bayern Munich means he’ll be playing in Germany until 2029.

He’s played for England 41 times since he left Tottenham Hotspur and the Premier League behind in 2023.

That means he only needs to play 14 more times to equal, or 15 times to beat, David Beckham’s record for the most caps earned while not playing club football in England.

55 of Beckham’s caps came after he left Manchester United to embark on a career with Real Madrid, LA Galaxy and AC Milan (he had retired from international football by the time he joined his last club, PSG).

You’d imagine Kane will play way more than 15 times for England between now and 2029.

Believe it or not, Kane hasn’t scored a hat-trick for England for five years now, last doing so in November 2021 against San Marino.

But it was his fifth international hat-trick and only Jimmy Greaves has more for England with six.

Could Kane get two more to overtake him? That might require some luck of the draw with qualifying for tournaments, pitting England against weaker teams, but he’s got enough time to try.

He does it often enough at club level, after all.

Even if he just gets one more hat-trick to match Greaves, he’d stand alone as the oldest hat-trick scorer for England.

That’s currently Jack Rowley at 31 years and 40 days old in 1949. It’s been a long-standing record, but Kane would instantly set a new one if he was to score an international hat-trick at any point from now.

Another one that might need some luck of the draw, but Kane has played seven times against Croatia in his England career, including on his record-breaking cap.

The only man to have played against a single, non-British opponent more is Alan Ball, who played eight times against West Germany between 1965 and 1975.

England and Croatia seem to meet every other week, so although the international schedule beyond this break remains unclear, there’s every chance Kane will cross paths with them again.

On a similar note, the most anyone has scored against a single non-British opponent for England is eight, by Vivian Woodward against Austria between 1908 and 1909.

Kane’s most common victims have been Albania (seven goals) and Croatia (six goals). If he plays against either of them again once or twice, he might fancy his chances.

#1468. The top goalscorers for club & country in 2026 so far: Kane, Yamal, Mbappe, Raphinha…

Big names from Real Madrid, Barcelona, Arsenal and Bayern Munich feature alongside some surprise names in the most prolific goalscorers of the calendar year so far.

Some big names are surprisingly absent from the most prolific goalscorers of 2026 to date.

Drawn from Europe’s five major leagues, here are the top 10 goalscorers in 2026 across club and international competitions.

Dembele has scored 20 goals in 36 PSG appearances this year, including several crucial strikes in Europe – none bigger than the equalising spot kick he coolly dispatched against Arsenal in the Champions League final.

His goal in France’s World Cup win over Iraq was, incredibly, his first in major tournament football. That was swiftly followed up with a rapid hat-trick against Norway, before another in the quarter-final against Morocco.

He is largely taking it easy right now, once again frequently rested during PSG’s domestic campaign. But he popped up with a goal against Manchester City.

Schick has had reason to celebrate in 2026. Earlier this year, he reached the milestone of 100 goals for Bayer Leverkusen.

He’s been on fire this season, with 12 goals from 14 games for the German side.

There won’t be any more international goals from Schick, though. He retired from Czech Republic duty after the World Cup.

The jury is still out on Gyokeres, who remains a perplexing forward.

This calendar year has seen him look borderline anonymous and increasingly sidelined at Arsenal.

And yet Gyokeres also fired Sweden to the World Cup with a hat-trick against Ukraine and a late winner against Poland. He’s basically the Ikea Gerd Muller at this point.

What a year it’s been for Malen. Started it as a benchwarmer at Aston Villa. Set to finish it as one of Europe’s most lethal strikers at Roma.

Malen made an immediate impact after his January move to the Italian capital and his scoring rate has barely slowed down since.

For some reason, his form hasn’t quite translated into international football; he hasn’t scored for the Netherlands at all this year.

But high-flying Roma are laughing. Malen almost won the Serie A golden boot last season despite arriving midway through and he’s a leading contender for the gong this season.

A fairly recent entrant into the top 10 after heading into the international break on the back of a hat trick against Union Berlin.

Olise was the Bundesliga’s best assister last season but has been more than capable of finding the net himself a fair few times too.

He didn’t score any goals at the World Cup but netted the winner in Zinedine Zidane’s second game in charge of France. The best Fantasy Footballer around right now.

Yamal has long been talked up as a Ballon d’Or contender, and slowly but surely he’s getting the numbers to back it up.

The teenager’s goalscoring output has grown season on season, and 2025-26 was no exception. February’s hat-trick against Villarreal was evidence of a player about to go truly stratospheric.

Unfortunately, the final furlong of the campaign was hit by a hamstring injury, or else we suspect he’d be a few places higher up in this list.

He needed just 10 minutes in his first World Cup start to find the back of the net, although that would be his only goal in Spain’s triumph out in North America.

Now he’s looking fit and hungry – at least based on the evidence of his exceptional form of late.

The Brazilian has an exceptional tally of 33 goals for Barcelona so far this calendar year (plus one for Brazil), which is especially impressive when you consider he’s missed quite a lot of action due to injury.

He averages a goal every 49 minutes for Barca this season – to put that in context, Kylian Mbappe averages a goal every 84 minutes for Real Madrid.

Raphinha has scored in all but three of the Barca games he’s played in in 2026-27, scoring hat tricks in two, and currently leads the Europe-wide goalscoring charts with 15 in the league.

The top three are the last three winners of the European Golden Shoe. This list has taken a while to take shape, but the frontrunners are the usual suspects.

Haaland’s four goals against Iraq and Senegal in the group stages finally saw him climb up into the top 10, from which he was surprisingly absent in the latter half of the 2025-26 club season, before he added to his World Cup tally against the Ivory Coast. Then there were two goals against Brazil.

He finally drew a blank as Norway exited the World Cup at the hands of England at the quarter-final stage. He earned a well-deserved rest before spearheading Man City’s new era under Enzo Maresca.

Same as it ever was with nine goals in nine Premier League appearances for City this season, plus braces against Porto and PSG and another Champions League goal against his favourite opponents, RB Leipzig.

Like his rival Haaland, it somehow took Mbappe until mid-June to enter the top 10.

Mbappe kicked off the year in superb style, scoring in six successive starts for Real Madrid (nine goals in total) before dipping considerably with just one goal in his next seven appearances.

By the nature of his 10 goals at the World Cup, we don’t expect to see the Real Madrid superstar dropping back out. His Champions League record is pretty sensational.

Arguably the finest player in world football right now. How often have you been able to say that about an Englishman?

The only player in Europe’s five major leagues to average a better-than-goal-a-game output so far this calendar year, the England captain has 41 goals in 40 appearances for Bayern Munich in all competitions in 2026 – including home and away against Real Madrid and PSG.

He capped off his superb season with a hat-trick in the DFB Pokal final. Two goals against Croatia showed Kane carried his form into the World Cup, where he eventually scored six times.

Unbelievably, the Norway game was Kane’s first knockout appearance for club and country in 2025-26 in which he didn’t score. Which, of course, he followed with a blank against Argentina.

Surprisingly enough, Kane failed to add to his tally by drawing a blank in his first three Bayern appearances of the 2026-27 campaign.

But it’s back to normal service with his Bayern tally standing at 10 goals in 14 games. The Czechs and Croatia have been on the receiving end in the Nations League too.

Still some way to go before catching Lionel Messi’s calendar year record, mind.

#1467. Journaling, no days off and 'Mamba Mentality': How Senne Lammens is trying to arrest his slide in form - and why his Man United team-mates must take the blame for his shattered confidence

Published: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026

Senne Lammens will have gone home on Sunday night, picked up his journal and tried to make sense of where it all went horribly wrong.

Journaling is what keeps Lammens’ mind at ease and what allows him to move on from moments of disappointment, of which Sunday afternoon against Aston Villa will have ranked high on his list.

Lammens may have lamented his decision to use his knees, rather than his hands, in attempting to deal with Alysson’s strike in the first minute. And that he parried a shot straight to Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 three minutes later. Lammens is big on accountability. Nobody will have needed to tell him that he could have done much better.

The responsibility for Villa goals three and four, however, lands squarely at the feet of his team-mates, a familiar pattern across the season so far.

Still, this was Lammens' worst performance in a Manchester United shirt, and the player himself is unlikely to have come to a different conclusion. But he has not become a bad goalkeeper overnight. Far from it.

While there was plenty of attention on his two costly mistakes against Villa, many have seemingly forgotten about a crucial one-on-one save Lammens made to deny Julio Enciso in the opening home match against Ipswich Town. It was 0-0 then and United would go on to win 5-2.

Senne Lammens has had a difficult start to the season - and was partly at fault for two of the goals Manchester United conceded in Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

They have forgotten two brilliant saves he made at Fulham to deny Sander Berge, and then Josh King. The second, with his right foot, was sublime and kept a listing United in the game at 0-0.

Even in United's season opener, the 24-year-old did tremendously well to push Oli McBurnie’s goalbound effort onto the post, only for three of his back four to switch off, allowing Hull City to score en route to a 2-0 win.

Overlooked are the failed defensive assignments of Bryan Mbeumo (against Ipswich Town), or Carlos Baleba (against Leeds United), or the costly mistakes of Lisandro Martinez, Diogo Dalot and Leny Yoro.

Lammens’ own form has regressed, there’s no doubt about that, but no goalkeeper in the Premier League is being sold short by those in front of him more than the United No 1 right now.

Across 10 Premier League matches, no goalkeeper has faced more shots on his goal than Lammens (52), tied in first place with Newcastle United’s Lukas Hornicek.

It’s also worth noting that no goalkeeper has made more saves in a single Premier League match this season than Lammens’ eight at Chelsea. United went on to lose 2-0 that day.

Lammens has made the fourth-most saves this season and yet has conceded a league-high 19 goals (Crystal Palace's 24 have been let in by both Walter Benitez and Dean Henderson).

Last season, across 32 games, Lammens faced 118 shots, averaging 3.69 per game. Fast forward to this campaign and it’s 52 shots in 10 games, up to 5.2 per game, a stark increase in workload.

Only twice last season did Lammens face six or more shots in a Premier League game. This season it has happened four times already.

Lammens had a rush of the blood to the head when he came out – and missed out – as Evanilson knocked the ball past him to score Bournemouth’s third at Old Trafford last month

Mistakes, such as those at Everton, Fulham and at home to Villa, are costly. His distribution, too, has become a sore spot with Lammens ranking 15th of 16 ever-present goalkeepers for completed long passes (37 of 115 attempted).

But Lammens performed well in the last international break for Belgium behind competent defenders. He doesn’t have that luxury at United right now.

‘Sometimes in the end it comes down to maybe here and there, maybe a mistake from someone, but it doesn’t really start with that,’ Lammens said of United's defensive issues earlier this season.

‘I think it’s a team thing. The manager has been hammering a lot about defending as a team, being able to put pressure on the opposition team, especially on crosses.’

A key selling point for Lammens last season was the composure he brought and the calmness he exuded. He was everything to United that Andre Onana wasn’t. That’s been chipped away this season.

A nervousness has crept in. The misplaced pass against Tottenham Hotspur to Kobbie Mainoo that was never on, which saw him redeem himself with a strong save from Dominic Solanke. The rush of blood to come out – and miss out – as Evanilson knocked the ball past him to score Bournemouth’s third at Old Trafford. The judgment call to use his legs as the ball ricocheted off Martinez and into his own net at Fulham.

All of which has led to a pundit and social media pile-on of a goalkeeper that, in the eyes of some, is now out of his depth.

Which is where the journaling comes in. It helps Lammens' belief that things will turn for the better, and the composure of a man who didn’t get too high when he was anointed the Signing of the Season for 2025-26 across the entire Premier League, and who isn’t getting too low about the most scrutinised run of his career.

‘Especially at big clubs, you don't want a keeper who performs well one match and poorly the next,’ Lammens said back in September.

‘You want someone who is a rock behind the defence. Someone the team can rely on. That's definitely a major goal for me. It's something to embody as a goalkeeper.

‘You can compare it a bit to Edwin van der Sar. He's someone I admire greatly. What I want to take from his game is that calmness.’

Lammens' confidence was rocked by a mistake he made in Belgium's World Cup exit to Spain - and United's leaky defence has left him unable to build it back up

The 24-year-old is known to pass up days off to put in extra work, and sources say he is first in in the morning and last to head home at the end of training

Lammens is known to pass up days off to put in extra work, and sources say he is first in in the morning and last to head home at the end of training. There are even figures at United who believe parts of his game have improved on last season.

His confidence was rocked in the summer when his spill to Mikel Merino sent Belgium home from the World Cup and he has had little chance to build back that confidence given the storm back in Manchester.

Basketball legend Kobe Bryant is Lammens' idol. He sports the late LA Lakers star's numbers on his gloves and swears by his 'Mamba Mentality'. And if that mentality tells us anything, it’s that resilience and fearlessness win out.

Lammens is struggling but he’s still the same goalkeeper that was being lauded last season. He just needs a helping hand from those in front of him or this defence will be stuck in a never-ending cycle of misery.

#1466. Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool

Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

He needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

When Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

Cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

“A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

“Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose said. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola said: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”

Jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

"Let's go! One of many!" Virgil van Dijk giving Jérémy Jacquet his POTM award after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/6xWvjmrF8Y

"That's a big moment to me to play with Virgil!" 🫡Jérémy Jacquet after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth! pic.twitter.com/UsTimGME39

Cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young said on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose big players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”

Fair play to anyone who retained Brobbey in their Fantasy Football teams this week...

4 - Brian Brobbey is the fourth player in Premier League history to score a hat-trick against the side starting the day top of the table, after Robbie Fowler v Aston Villa in November 1998, Dirk Kuyt v Man Utd in March 2011, and Romelu Lukaku v Man Utd in May 2013.Unstoppable. pic.twitter.com/vygVYazIQD

Maresca’s side maintain their immaculate record, but boy were they made to work for it this afternoon.

Sunderland are still 5-3 down but have not given up the ghost. Surely the best match of the season so far?

It ends goalless at Elland Road after Mitchell’s goal was disallowed for offside. Kamada went close to breaking the deadlock in the final stages...

Daichi Kamada can't guide his header on target! ❌ pic.twitter.com/AgKM6Q9apq

Bournemouth lose at the Vitality for the first time in 13 matches as Iraola makes a winning return to the South Coast. Liverpool were hardly impressive, but to their credit they managed the final stages of this match with a minimum of fuss.

Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium with a win! ✅ pic.twitter.com/FSgvE6EGFB

Bournemouth are awarded a corner but Brooks’ delivery goes straight into the inviting gloves of Alisson.

Koumas pressures Petrovic, but the goalkeeper shows off some tidy footwork to escape the danger.

Bournemouth cannot get out though, and Petrovic is forced into a routine save off Koumas moments later.

Bournemouth win a free-kick in a dangerous position after a handball, but Scott cannot get his strike up and down fast enough and it sails over.

Haaland gets in on the act, but only after a VAR check. That should be that...

Erling Haaland has now scored against all 25 teams he has faced in the Premier League ✅⚽ pic.twitter.com/X9uqcrgbwk

Araujo gets his pocket picked in the corner but Jebbison cannot compose himself and blasts his cross off the other side of the pitch.

Liverpool go the other way and win a corner, but Mac Allister puts too much air on his delivery and it is easily dealt with.

Rayan wins a free-kick as he holds off Kerkez on the halfway line. Bournemouth then switch play to the far side but Truffert’s speculative effort flies well over the bar.

Nyoni shows off his composure on the ball, playing simple passes on the half-turn to keep play flowing. The midfield area is quite congested, which suits Liverpool at this point in the game.

Liverpool are baiting Bournemouth’s press in an attempt to play around their front line. They are doing a good job at holding on to the ball and frustrating their opponents, for now.

Gravenberch and Koumas are on for Gakpo and Isak.

Brooks has brought some energy to Bournemouth’s forays down the left. He attempts to slip a ball into the left channel but Nyoni is wise to it and positions himself perfectly to cut it out.

Liverpool have dropped deep and Bournemouth wait patiently for an opening. They eventually find Tavernier in the left half-space but his cross flies over everyone.

That is his last contribution to the match as Rose rings the changes: Tavernier, Smith and Christie make way for Brooks, Jebbison and Cook.

Truffert spins in a teasing ball from the left but Jacquet does well to flick the ball away from the danger zone.

Wirtz and Barcola make way for Nyoni and Munoz. Quiet afternoon from both of the outgoing players.

A stunning block from Hill prevents Isak pulling trigger as he looked to have the goal in his sights.

Truffert clears the resulting corner to safety.

Isak is concentrating his efforts in more central areas and here he almost gets played in behind but the ball just runs away from him. Better.

Worth mentioning that Jacquet has been fantastic in all phases of the game. Plenty of advanced regains and tidy passes forward.

It’s raining goals in Manchester and no prizes for guessing who has scored for Sunderland. Brobbey has his hat-trick.

Brobbey has his hat-trick and the look on Enzo Maresca’s face as he assesses the defending from his team. They’ve been great pouring forward, less so trying to stymie Sunderand’s attack. But this is one of those games where you just sit back and enjoy the unfolding drama. It’s been so good from both teams.

Semenyo gets his second goal of the afternoon to extend the league leaders’ advantage.

Chance! Jacquet jumps and wins the ball well inside Bournemouth’s half and his intervention sends the ball into Isak’s path. The forward just drags his effort wide and turns out he was in an offside postion anyhow.

What an afternoon this is turning out to be. There have been more slices than on an erratic day on the local municipal golf course and Ronald Araujo is the latest to be afflicted by the condition. None of that will matter to Andoni Iraola, though, as Alexander Isak’s fourth goal in four Premier League games has given Liverpool a huge advantage. They haven’t played with fluency but the breakthrough was significant.

Isak opens the scoring at the Vitality, finally getting into the box and sweeping in from close range. So much credit has to go to Gakpo who tiptoes past two Bournemouth defenders by the touchline before spearing a cross infield, and while he may not be attributed with the assist owing to a touch off Wirtz, his delivery makes it all the way through to Isak who taps in.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

Adams has been superb as one of Bournemouth’s two midfield sentries. Kerkez looks to have been played into the left channel but the American swoops in and shields the ball out of play before staring down his Hungarian opponent.

Mitchell thinks he’s given the visitors the lead but his goal is ruled out for offside.

Tyrick Mitchell's opener is disallowed for an offside in the build up! ❌ pic.twitter.com/7y975TxaUj

Liverpool give up possession in Bournemouth’s half and Christie strides forward releasing Rayan before continuing his run to the near post. The Brazilian picks out his team-mate but Christie gets too strong a contact on the ball and the ball sails wide.

Truffert passes the ball straight to Gakpo inside his own box but Adams is on the scene in a flash and snaps into a tackle and takes the ball away from the Liverpool forward.

The second has already settled into a holding pattern, with neither side creating much. Isak makes a run down the right hand side and, with players loaded in the box, he blasts the ball high into the sky and beyond his team-mates. That pretty much sums things up.

Wirtz has given the ball away twice in the first minute of the second half. Carragher is on Sky Sports commentary duties and he says he’s surprised to see him back out on the pitch.

Szoboszlai concedes a foul on the far side but the subsequent delivery is too heavy and sails over everyone.

No half-time changes from either manager.

3 - This is the first time that @ManCity have taken the lead three times in the first half of a Premier League match.Overall, it's just the seventh time in competition history that a side has gone ahead on three separate occasions in a first half.Canvas. pic.twitter.com/JaQ4qDarls

Isak’s first-half heatmap makes for interesting reading. The good news, for Liverpool fans, is that he’s stationed himself predominantly in the final third. The bad news... those positions have been everywhere but the box.

There must be significant temptation to drift out to the wide areas and drop deep when the ball is not coming to you, but surely Liverpool need their No 9 closer to Bournemouth’s goal?

Bournemouth 0 Liverpool 0Leeds United 0 Crystal Palace 0 Manchester City 3 Sunderland 2

Big chance missed from Haaland of all people to make it 4-2 to City in what has been a pulsating, spell-binding first 45 minutes. It’s fast, furious and a helluva lot of fun to watch. Brilliant from Ndiaye to tee up Haaland who shoots wide of a post. A game for attackers shall we say ...

There are significant advantages to having a goalkeeper who is 6ft 5in with long arms and massive hands. Brobbey’s shot cannons off Guehi and would have looped over a number of goalkeeper but Donnarumma sticks out a giant arm to help nudge the ball over the bar and keep City 3-2 in front in the fifth minute of first half stoppages

Not a pretty half from the returning Iraola’s side, who will need to be much better in the second period to challenge for the three points.

Bournemouth have dropped points late on in a number of matches this season and will perhaps rue not being able to capitalise on their early advantage.

City are in front. Again. Semenyo this time, he fires the ball beyond Roefs having collected a loose ball int he box.

Antoine Semenyo gets his first goal of the season! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/1n2W5Cyxz0

A relatively slick Liverpool move sees the ball worked out to Araujo on the right who has minded to bomb on with increasing frequency, and while he’s able to win a corner, Szoboszlai’s delivery is cleared with a minimum of fuss.

Iraola came into this game saying that his side held an advantage having played two days earlier than Bournemouth in midweek. You would never have guessed it from what we have witnessed here today.

And right on cue, a frustrated Isak attempts a specultative effort from range which sails high and wide.

Sunderland are level again as Brobbey scores after lengthy VAR check for offside.

Sunderland fans sing “F--- VAR” and City fans boo the delay while they both awaited the verdict, which has now gone Sunderland’s way

Brian Brobbey levels it AGAIN! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/YvelzwnmY8

Can’t hold a lead today City. Wow, Sunderland are level again in an instant and it’s that man Brobbey again. There’s a VAR check going on to check for offside

So, this is not a rush to make a sweeping criticism, it’s simply an observation. But Liverpool fans will be looking at Bradley Barcola and  waiting to see that first burst, that moment of electricity, that has showed why they bought him. It’s like you look for a touch, a pass, a moment of skill. He’s just had a shot saved but it all seems very tentative for him at the moment. And that is what he needs - a moment.

Jacquet does brilliantly to close down Christie as the Scot was stealing into the box and looking to pull the trigger.

Chances! Barcola forces Petrovic into an awkward-looking save, before follow-up efforts from Wirtz and Gakpo are charged down.

Mac Allister is fouled 25 yards out moments later and Szoboszlai gets another go. Here, he drags his effort just wide.

It’s all happening at the Etihad. Cherki restores City’s lead with his third Premier League goal of the season.

It’s a great finish from Cherki to put City back in front but it doesn’t happen if Ndiaye is quick to read Danso’s risky pass and win possession. Sharp as a button in that moment.

Rayan Cherki puts Manchester City back in front! 💫 pic.twitter.com/PP4MAV9kw3

A really poor piece of defending from Kerkez gives Bournemouth a free-kick out on the right. Tavernier spins in an inswinger but Van Dijk heads clear. Truffert launches another assault on Liverpool’s box off the second phase but Alisson is wise to it and gathers.

It appears that Liverpool are beginning to settle, they take the opportunity to circulate the ball in front of Bournemouth’s first line of pressure, waiting for the right moment to pounce. The final pass is poor, though, and Araujo through-pass goes all the way through to Petrovic. It was aimed at Isak ...I think.

Some signs of life from Liverpool, as they create a substantial overload down their left, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Barcola and Isak meeting on that flank.
